rewrites.summary:
Tocantins stands entirely under Brazil's nationally uniform framework: marriage equality since 2013, name and gender-marker change at the registry without surgery since 2018, homophobia and transphobia criminalised as equivalent to racism by the Supreme Court in 2019, and non-binary civil-registry amendments allowed by a 2025 superior-court ruling — protections built by the courts rather than statute, with repeal efforts active in Congress bearing on their stability.

No Tocantins-specific statute, ordinance or enforcement pattern is on file. A Brazilian law-firm guide records that the legal rights are identical nationwide while major cities are broadly welcoming and smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction — a distinction that reaches through Tocantins as elsewhere.

Brazil continues to have one of the highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities, particularly trans people; that national profile, not any local divergence, sets the state's risk. Over 3,000 openly LGBTQ candidates ran in the 2024 municipal elections, evidencing political visibility at local level nationally.

rewrites.summary:
Puducherry is a union territory with a partial legislature: recognition and welfare policy for trans people is set principally by the federal government, and no Puducherry-specific statute, enforcement series or incident pattern is on file.

The framework that governs it shifted sharply in March 2026: parliament passed an amendment removing the self-identification right affirmed by the 2014 Supreme Court ruling, restricting legal recognition to historically recognised communities (hijra/kinnar) and intersex people, mandating medical certification for identity documents and for surgery; critics and a court-appointed advisory panel warn it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people, protests followed the vote in several cities, and the change bears uniformly on every state and territory.

Nationally recurring policing practice — treating trans appearance as a suspicion category in transit spaces, evidenced by an August 2024 railway-platform groping complaint (an FIR was filed and intrusive questioning reported) — reaches union-territory visitors through federal transport policing rather than any local law.

rewrites.summary:
No Mizoram-specific trans statute or enforcement record is on file; the union of national law governs recognition here. In March 2026 that national framework narrowed significantly: both houses passed an amendment to the 2019 trans persons law removing self-identification, restricting legal recognition to biologically-verified and traditional-community categories, and mandating medical-board certification for gender-affirming surgery. The bill drew nationwide protests from the community and opposition parties, a Supreme Court-appointed advisory panel asked the government to withdraw it, and presidential assent remained pending as of late March 2026.

Neither international reporting on the change nor any other source on file records Mizoram-level deviation — statute, ban, or enforcement campaign — in either direction; the northeast state's day-to-day exposure for a trans visitor therefore runs through the central framework, its pending narrowing included.

rewrites.summary:
Manipur sits under India's national framework with no region-specific trans statute, ban or enforcement campaign reported. That framework narrowed on 26 March 2026: both houses passed an amendment to the 2019 Transgender Persons Act removing the self-identification right affirmed by the 2014 Supreme Court ruling, restricting legal recognition to historically recognised communities (hijra/kinner) and intersex people, and requiring medical-board certification — with a new offence carrying up to life imprisonment for coercing someone into transition per human-rights reporting. Recognition is already thin in practice: about 32,500 of the census-recorded 487,803 transgender persons hold ID cards. A court-appointed advisory panel sought withdrawal amid protests; assent was pending.

The country dossier's reporting on the amendment explicitly notes no Manipur-specific deviation — the recognition machinery, the certification requirement and the new offence apply to the state exactly as elsewhere in India, which is what sets a visitor's exposure there.

rewrites.summary:
Bremen has no trans-specific statute, ordinance or enforcement series of its own on file. The city-state operates Germany's federal framework: the Self-Determination Act, in force since 1 November 2024, remains operative as of September 2026, and registry changes run through Bremen's own offices; federal criminal law and the general equality act apply unchanged.

Two framework-level developments matter for trans people everywhere in Germany through state competence over prisons: a July 2026 court-ordered placement of a trans-woman-registered prisoner in a men's prison (the widely reported 'Liebich' case) drove three eastern states into a Bundesrat initiative to tighten the Self-Determination Act; and a March 2026 constitutional-law survey found most Länder anchoring newly reformed prison-placement codes to the registry sex entry — Bremen is not among the states named as having rewritten its code, and no Bremen-specific detention finding is on file.

rewrites.summary:
Hamburg has no hostile-offence series, ordinance or event-security finding on file; risk tracks Germany's federal framework, with one local exception that is institutional rather than social: Hamburg is among the Länder whose newly reformed prison-placement rules have entered into force, tying inmate placement to the civil-registry sex entry — a March 2026 constitutional-law survey counts it alongside the first wave of rewrites (a Rhineland-Palatinate code effective 1 March 2026, Bavaria, Saxony) and argues the registry-anchored approach is constitutionally avoidable and in part doubtful on fundamental-rights grounds.

The framework around it moved in July 2026: a court-ordered placement of a trans-woman-registered prisoner in a men's facility (the reported 'Liebich' case, arising in the northeast, corroborated by multiple wire reports of 15-17 July 2026) sharpened pressure that produced a Bundesrat initiative to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act, itself in force since November 2024. For a visitor, detention-time placement — not street-level hostility — is where Hamburg's documented divergence lies, and it is a resident-facing machinery a arrested visitor would enter.
